title: How to find your first 100 readers before launch day
summary: A plain plan for building a small, real group of readers who will buy, read and talk about your book in its first week.

body.p: Most first books don't fail because they're bad. They fail because nobody knows they exist on launch day. The fix isn't a big ad budget. It's 100 people who already care when the book goes live.

100 is small enough to reach with your own hands and big enough to matter. If even a third of them buy in launch week and a handful leave honest reviews, your book page stops looking empty. An empty page is the hardest thing to sell from.

body.h: Step 1: Write down who you already know

body.p: Open a note in your Author Studio and list everyone who would be happy for you: friends, family, coworkers, church or club members, old classmates, people you follow and talk with online. Don't judge the list yet. Most authors are surprised to find 60 to 150 names.

body.h: Step 2: Sort them into three groups

list: Will read it: people who read your kind of book.
Will share it: people who don't read the genre but love to cheer you on.
Can open a door: someone with a podcast, a newsletter, a book club, a store or a big following.

body.p: Each group gets a different ask. Readers get an early copy. Sharers get a ready-to-post message. Door-openers get a short, personal pitch.

body.h: Step 3: Give them a reason to say yes

body.p: Ask a small, specific favor with a date on it. "Would you read an early copy and, if you like it, post one honest line about it the week of March 1?" works far better than "please support my book."

body.tip: Never ask anyone for a 5-star review. Ask for an honest one. Stores like Amazon remove reviews that look arranged, and honesty protects your name.

body.h: Step 4: Collect emails, not just likes

body.p: A social post is seen by a few people for a few hours. An email reaches the inbox. Use any free email-list tool and add everyone who says yes. On launch day you'll send one message and know it arrives.

Between now and launch, send something small every two to three weeks: the cover, a favorite line, a photo of the proof copy, a thank-you. People who watch a book come together feel part of it, and those are the people who buy.

list: Mark each name read, share or door.
Add every yes to your email list.
